lead: A lamp turns electrical power into light. Its efficacy is the light output per watt, in lumens per watt (lm/W). Halogen, gas-discharge and LED sources differ mainly in that number, in colour and in how fast they start. Car makers choose among them for headlamps, tail lamps and indicators. This chapter compares the sources and the lamp units built around them. Only a few universities teach this topic.
prereq: You need: P = V I from Unit 1, Batteries, Starting and Charging Systems.

blocks.text: Light is measured in four linked units. Luminous flux Φ is total light output, in lumens (lm). Luminous intensity I is flux per solid angle, in candela (cd = lm/sr). Illuminance E is flux falling on a surface, in lux (lux = lm/m²). Luminance L is intensity per unit area, in cd/m²; it is what the eye sees as the brightness of a surface. Efficacy η is flux per electrical watt: η = Φ / P, in lm/W. Here Φ is luminous flux in lm, P is electrical power in W. A 55 W halogen bulb giving 1500 lm has η = 1500/55 = 27.3 lm/W. Spreading the same 1500 lm over a wider beam does not make the lamp brighter on the road; it lowers illuminance at each point.

Filament lamps use incandescence: current heats a tungsten wire to about 2700 K, and it glows. Plain tungsten gives roughly 10–15 lm/W. A halogen lamp adds iodine or bromine vapour; the halogen cycle returns evaporated tungsten to the filament, so the bulb runs hotter and lasts longer, at about 20–30 lm/W. Gas-discharge lamps strike an arc through gas. HID xenon lamps use a xenon fill and metal salts; they give about 80 lm/W and a bluish-white colour, but need a ballast and take seconds to reach full output. Solid-state lamps use electroluminescence: electrons recombine with holes in a semiconductor junction and release photons. LEDs give about 90–110 lm/W, start instantly and last long. Laser headlamps use blue lasers and a phosphor to make a very small, very bright source.

blocks.text: A bare source is not a headlamp. A reflector collects the light and shapes it into a beam. A projector unit uses an ellipsoidal reflector, a lens and a cut-off shield; the shield creates the sharp horizontal cut-off that keeps light out of oncoming drivers' eyes. A lens, or the reflector surface, spreads or focuses the beam. The beam pattern is asymmetric. In left-hand-drive countries, where traffic keeps right, the beam is low and short on the left, towards oncoming traffic, and rises on the right to light the near-side kerb without glare. In India, where traffic keeps left, the pattern is mirrored: the dip is on the right and the rise on the left. Demands: enough flux on the road, no glare above the cut-off, short warm-up, long life, vibration resistance and low cost. Halogen is cheap and instant; HID gives more light but needs a ballast and warm-up; LED is efficient and durable but needs heat management and careful optics.

examples.question: A halogen headlamp uses a 55 W bulb giving 1500 lm. An LED headlamp gives 2000 lm for 20 W. The system runs at 13.2 V while charging. Find the efficacy of each and the current each draws.
steps: The LED gives 500 lm more flux for 35 W less power.
examples.answer: Halogen: 27.27 lm/W at 4.17 A; LED: 100.0 lm/W at 1.52 A; the LED gives 33% more flux for 2.65 A less current.

traps: Lumen, candela and lux are not interchangeable: lumen is total output, candela is output per direction, lux is light falling on a surface.
A higher-lumen lamp spread over a wider beam can put less light on the road; compare illuminance at the same distance.
HID xenon is not an LED: it needs a ballast and warm-up, and its colour comes from the arc, not a phosphor.
Halogen efficacy is 20–30 lm/W, not 80; 80 lm/W is HID.

quiz.q: Define luminous flux and give its unit.
quiz.a: Luminous flux is total light output; unit lumen (lm).

quiz.q: Why does a halogen lamp last longer than a plain tungsten lamp?
quiz.a: The halogen cycle returns evaporated tungsten to the filament, so less wire is lost.

quiz.q: A 35 W HID lamp gives 2800 lm. Find its efficacy.
A 1000 lm LED and a 1500 lm halogen use the same reflector. Why might the halogen still look brighter on the road?
quiz.a: With the same reflector the beam shape is similar, so the halogen's 1500 lm gives about 1.5 times the illuminance (lux) of the 1000 lm LED; efficacy sets the current drawn, not the light on the road.

quiz.q: Name the three light-generation principles in car lamps.
What does a cut-off shield do in a projector headlamp?
quiz.a: It blocks the upper part of the beam to give a sharp cut-off and reduce glare to oncoming drivers.

beyond: Not for the exam. Matrix headlamps use many LEDs switched individually to blank out oncoming cars. Laser headlamps use blue lasers and a phosphor; they are not yet common. Research is on micro-LED arrays and adaptive driving beams. Search terms: adaptive driving beam, matrix LED, laser headlamp, photometric test.
